summary.name: Free software
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article defining free software (libre software) as computer software licensed so users can run, study, change, and redistribute it, and covering its history, licenses, and the GNU Project.
use_cases: learning history of the free software movement
understanding business models for free software
summary.what_it_does: The page explains that free software is distributed under licenses granting users the freedom to run, study, change, and distribute it, and frames this as a matter of liberty rather than price. It lists the four essential freedoms from the Free Software Foundation's definition and contrasts free software with proprietary software and freeware. It describes the history from the 1950s through the GNU Project (1983), the FSF (1985), and the Linux kernel's GPL relicensing (1992). It also surveys common licenses (MIT, GPL, Apache, BSD, LGPL, MPL, Eclipse) and the categories of public-domain, permissive, and copyleft licensing.
notable: Defines the four essential freedoms (freedom 0 to 3) from the Free Software Foundation
Distinguishes free software from open source, with the FSF's reasoning
Covers copyleft versus permissive licensing debates
Traces history from the GNU Project to the Linux kernel and BSD derivatives
caveats: Encyclopedia article, not a software tool; it describes concepts rather than a downloadable product
Some views on licensing and security are presented as contested debate rather than settled fact
